notes: PDF text date is partially garbled by extraction; lead and document context show June 8, 2023.
title: Order on Artificial Intelligence
court: United States Court of International Trade
summary: Judge Stephen Alexander Vaden of the Court of International Trade requires any party filing AI-drafted text in his cases to provide a notice identifying the generative AI program and the specific drafted portions, and to certify that no confidential or business proprietary information was disclosed to an unauthorized party.
key_provisions: Applies to submissions in cases assigned to Judge Vaden containing text drafted with generative AI based on natural language prompts.
Names ChatGPT and Google Bard as examples of covered generative AI programs.
Requires a disclosure notice identifying the program used and the specific portions of text drafted with it.
Requires certification that use of the program did not disclose confidential or business proprietary information to unauthorized parties.
Allows any party to seek relief under statute or USCIT rules after the notice is filed.

notes: Lead list had an earlier 2024 date; the current court PDF is dated July 24, 2025.
title: Order on Artificial Intelligence
court: United States Court of International Trade
summary: Judge Claire R. Kelly of the Court of International Trade requires filings in her cases that contain text drafted with generative AI to include a disclosure identifying the program and portions drafted, plus a certification that confidential or business proprietary information was not disclosed to unauthorized parties.
key_provisions: Applies to any submission in a case assigned to Judge Kelly containing text drafted with generative AI based on natural language prompts.
Identifies ChatGPT and Google Bard as nonexclusive examples of covered tools.
Requires a disclosure notice identifying the program used and the specific portion of text drafted.
Requires a certification that no confidential or business proprietary information was disclosed to unauthorized parties.
Permits parties to file motions seeking relief based on the disclosed facts.

text_excerpt: "ORDERED that any submission in a case assigned to Judge Restani that contains text drafted with the assistance of a generative artificial intelligence program" must be accompanied by notice and certification.
notes: Lead list had an earlier 2024 date; the current court PDF is dated July 24, 2025.
title: Order on Artificial Intelligence
court: United States Court of International Trade
summary: Judge Jane A. Restani of the Court of International Trade requires AI-drafted text in submissions in her cases to be disclosed by program and text portion, and requires certification that use of the generative AI program did not disclose confidential or business proprietary information to unauthorized parties.
key_provisions: Applies to submissions in cases assigned to Judge Restani containing text drafted with generative AI based on natural language prompts.
Names ChatGPT and Google Bard as examples without limiting the order to those tools.
Requires a disclosure notice identifying the program used and the specific portion of text drafted.
Requires certification that use of the program did not disclose confidential or business proprietary information to an unauthorized party.
Provides that any party may file a motion seeking relief after the notice is filed.

text_excerpt: "A disclosure notice that identifies the program used, the manner in which it was used, and the specific portions of text that have been drafted" must accompany covered submissions.
title: Standing Order on the Use of Artificial Intelligence
court: United States Court of International Trade
summary: Judge Jennifer Choe-Groves of the Court of International Trade requires counsel and pro se litigants filing generative-AI-drafted text in her cases to disclose the program, manner of use, and portions drafted, certify human review for factual and legal accuracy, and certify no unauthorized disclosure of confidential information.
key_provisions: Applies to submissions in cases assigned to Judge Choe-Groves containing text drafted with the assistance of generative AI.
Requires a disclosure notice identifying the program used, the manner in which it was used, and the specific text portions drafted.
Requires certification that counsel or the party reviewed the included text and legal research for factual and legal accuracy.
Requires certification that use of the AI program did not cause unauthorized disclosure of confidential or business proprietary information.
Allows any party to move for appropriate relief after such a notice is filed.

text_excerpt: "Attorneys using generative artificial intelligence should be mindful of any individual chambers procedures or orders regarding confidential or business proprietary information" and Rule 11 obligations.
notes: Court-wide notice does not itself create a disclosure or certification duty beyond pointing to chambers orders and Rule 11.
title: Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Practice Before the Court
court: United States Court of International Trade
summary: The Court of International Trade posted a court-wide notice telling attorneys using generative AI to be mindful of individual chambers procedures or orders on confidential and business proprietary information and of Rule 11 obligations regarding representations made to the court.
key_provisions: The notice is directed to attorneys using generative artificial intelligence in practice before the Court of International Trade.
It points attorneys to individual chambers procedures or orders about confidential or business proprietary information.
It reminds attorneys of Rule 11 obligations concerning representations to the court.

sanctions_language: "A material misrepresentation in the certificate of compliance may result in striking the document and sanctions against the person signing the document."
text_excerpt: "counsel and unrepresented filers must further certify that no generative artificial intelligence program was used" or that generated text "has been reviewed for accuracy and approved by a human."
notes: The proposal text is undated; PDF metadata shows November 21, 2023 and comments were requested through January 4, 2024. The court declined to adopt it in 2024.
title: Notice of Proposed Amendment to Fifth Circuit Rule 32.3 and Form 6
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
summary: The Fifth Circuit proposed amending Rule 32.3 and Form 6 to require counsel and unrepresented filers to certify whether generative AI was used to draft a document and, if so, that generated text, citations, and legal analysis were reviewed for accuracy and approved by a human.
key_provisions: The proposal would have required counsel and unrepresented filers to certify AI use in the Rule 32.3 certificate of compliance.
Filers would certify either that no generative AI program was used or that AI-generated text was reviewed for accuracy.
The proposed Form 6 language covered generated text, citations, and legal analysis.
A material misrepresentation in the certificate could result in striking the document and sanctions.
The court later decided not to adopt a special rule governing generative AI.

sanctions_language: "I used AI” will not be an excuse for an otherwise sanctionable offense."
text_excerpt: "The court, having considered the proposed rule, the accompanying comments, and the use of artificial intelligence in the legal practice, has decided not to adopt a special rule" on AI drafting.
notes: PDF text is undated; PDF metadata shows June 11, 2024.
title: Court Decision on Proposed Rule
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
summary: The Fifth Circuit announced that it would not adopt a special rule on artificial intelligence in drafting briefs at that time, while reminding parties and counsel that existing appellate rules already require filings, including briefs, to be checked for truthfulness and accuracy.
key_provisions: The court considered the proposed rule, comments, and the use of artificial intelligence in legal practice.
The court decided not to adopt a special rule on artificial intelligence in drafting briefs at that time.
Parties and counsel remain responsible for ensuring that filings are truthful and accurate under existing rules.
The court stated that using AI will not excuse otherwise sanctionable conduct.

text_excerpt: "The guidance aims to allow for the use of and experimentation with AI tools while preserving the integrity and independence of the federal courts and the judicial process."
notes: Annual Report summarizes interim guidance; the full guidance document was not found publicly on uscourts.gov.
title: Developing Artificial Intelligence Policies
court: Federal Judiciary / Judicial Conference of the United States
summary: The Administrative Office reported that its advisory AI Task Force developed interim judiciary guidance for judges and staff that allows use and experimentation with AI tools while preserving court integrity and independence, cautions against delegating core judicial functions, and recommends independent verification of AI-generated output.
key_provisions: The AO established an advisory Artificial Intelligence Task Force in early 2025 with judges, court executives, IT staff, and chambers staff.
The task force is charged with coordinating AI issues for the judicial branch and recommending policies to the Judicial Conference.
The interim guidance aims to allow use and experimentation with AI while preserving federal court integrity and independence.
The guidance cautions against delegating core judicial functions to AI, including decision making and case adjudication.
The guidance recommends review and independent verification of all AI-generated content or output.

text_excerpt: "The evidence is admissible only if the proponent gives an adverse party reasonable notice of the intent to offer the evidence — so that the party has a fair opportunity to meet it."
notes: Report states proposed Rule 707 was released for public comment in August 2025; the May 2026 revised draft was not re-published pending further expert vetting.
title: Proposed Rule 707: Evidence Produced by Artificial Intelligence and Presented at Trial Without an Expert
court: Federal Rules of Evidence / Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules
summary: The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules reported a revised proposed Rule 707 that would regulate AI-produced evidence offered at trial without an expert witness, require the proponent to establish Rule 702-style reliability, ordinarily require expert explanation, and require reasonable notice to adverse parties.
key_provisions: Applies when evidence is a product of artificial intelligence and is offered without an expert witness but would be subject to Rule 702 if testified to by a witness.
Requires the proponent to establish helpfulness, sufficient facts or data, reliable principles and methods, and reliable application.
Ordinarily requires an expert to explain how the AI system reliably produced the evidence, with exceptional circumstances for other proof.
Makes the evidence admissible only if the proponent gives adverse parties reasonable notice of the intent to offer it.
The committee decided not to release the revised draft for a new public comment period at that time and planned further AI expert vetting.

text_excerpt: "a party claiming that an item is fabricated in whole or part by generative artificial intelligence must provide reasonable pretrial notice to all opposing parties" of intent to present fabrication evidence.
notes: This is a working draft held for further consideration, not a rule published for public comment as of the May 2026 report.
title: Working Draft Rule 901(c): Potentially Fabricated Evidence Created by Generative Artificial Intelligence
court: Federal Rules of Evidence / Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules
summary: The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules reported a working draft of Rule 901(c) for deepfake claims, requiring a party challenging evidence as fabricated by generative AI to make an evidentiary showing, shifting a higher authenticity burden to the proponent, and requiring reasonable pretrial notice of fabrication evidence.
key_provisions: A party challenging authenticity on the ground of generative-AI fabrication must present enough evidence to support a finding of fabrication.
If that showing is made, the item is admissible only if the proponent demonstrates it is more likely than not authentic.
The draft applies to items offered under either Rule 901 or Rule 902.
Unless the court orders otherwise, the party claiming generative-AI fabrication must provide reasonable pretrial notice to opposing parties.
The committee planned to seek input on whether the amendment should cover all AI, generative AI, and whether any amendment is necessary.

sanctions_language: "the court may take corrective action, including imposition of sanctions, if hallucinated content is submitted to the court."
text_excerpt: "I certify that I or an individual under my supervision has reviewed all content in this filing created with the assistance of generative artificial intelligence" for accurate authorities and support.
notes: This is a published rules suggestion submitted to the Civil Rules committee, not a committee-approved proposed amendment.
title: Rules Suggestion 25-CV-S: Proposed Rule 11(a) Generative AI Certification
court: Advisory Committee on Civil Rules / Committee on Rules of Practice and Procedure
summary: Rules Suggestion 25-CV-S asks the federal Civil Rules committee to consider amending Rule 11(a) so documents with citations and generative-AI-created content include a certification that supervised human review confirmed authorities exist, citations are accurate, and the authorities support the propositions cited.
key_provisions: The suggestion proposes a Rule 11(a) certification for any document containing citations filed with a court.
The proposed certification covers content created with the assistance of generative artificial intelligence.
The signer would certify that they or a supervised individual reviewed AI-created content for existing and accurately cited authorities.
The signer would certify that cited authorities support the propositions for which they are cited.
The proposed text acknowledges corrective action, including sanctions, for hallucinated content submitted to the court.

text_excerpt: "any paper submitted to the USPTO under signature must be reviewed by the person presenting the paper" and the reasonable inquiry can include verifying factual and legal representations.
notes: Administrative tribunal policy; memorandum says existing rules are adequate and announces forthcoming Federal Register guidance.
title: The Applicability of Existing Regulations as to Party and Practitioner Misconduct Related to the Use of Artificial Intelligence
court: Patent Trial and Appeal Board and Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, USPTO
summary: The USPTO Director advised the PTAB, TTAB, and General Counsel that existing regulations apply when parties and practitioners use AI in Board submissions, requiring signed papers to be reviewed by a person, accuracy of factual and legal representations verified, confidentiality protected, and sanctions available for misconduct.
key_provisions: The memorandum is addressed to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, and the Office of General Counsel.
Existing USPTO rules apply regardless of how a submission is generated, including with AI assistance.
Any paper submitted under signature must be reviewed by the person presenting the paper.
The reasonable inquiry can include determining how the paper was prepared and verifying factual and legal representations.
Sanctions may include striking papers, preclusion, affecting weight, terminating proceedings, criminal liability, and disciplinary action.

sanctions_language: "Failure to inquire when the circumstances warrant it could result in sanctions or other appropriate action."
text_excerpt: "there is no prohibition against using these computer tools in drafting documents for submission to the USPTO. Nor is there a general obligation to disclose to the USPTO the use of such tools."
notes: Administrative tribunal guidance; Federal Register notice states it does not create new rights or announce new USPTO practice, but personnel follow it if earlier guidance is inconsistent.
title: Guidance on Use of Artificial Intelligence-Based Tools in Practice Before the United States Patent and Trademark Office
court: United States Patent and Trademark Office, including PTAB and TTAB
summary: The USPTO guidance states that AI tools are not prohibited and generally need not be disclosed in USPTO practice, including PTAB and TTAB filings, but signed AI-assisted papers must be human reviewed, supported by reasonable inquiry, checked for factual and legal accuracy, and handled to protect confidentiality and USPTO systems.
key_provisions: The guidance applies to practice before the USPTO, including filings submitted to the PTAB and TTAB.
There is no prohibition against using computer tools, including generative AI, to draft documents for USPTO submission.
There is not presently a general duty to inform the USPTO that an AI tool was used unless specifically requested.
Any paper submitted to the USPTO must be reviewed by the party or parties presenting it, who remain responsible for the contents.
Parties should confirm facts, citations, legal contentions, and confidentiality obligations when AI tools are used.
AI systems may not obtain USPTO.gov accounts or apply a person’s signature without that person personally entering it.
